title: Why Great Leaders Plan to Change the Plan
author: The Business Leader Daily
source: The Business Leader Daily Substack, January 12, 2026
summary: Business Leader Daily argues that great leaders treat planning as a living discipline rather than an event, because even the best plans don't survive contact with shifting markets, faltering assumptions, and global, technological, or competitive disruption. The piece frames planning as both preparation (data, industry/market trends, evaluation of organizational resources) and institutionalization (consistent routines and dependable processes), and the right move when the inevitable upheaval comes is to focus on what's possible with the current information and develop a flexible framework that enables rapid reassessment and adjustment. The closing reframe: planning is an ongoing conversation, not a one-time declaration of intent. The piece anchors itself with quotes from Richard Rumelt (most strategic-planning exercises don't produce strategies but try to predict and control financial outcomes), Conchie & Dalton (high-performing leaders prioritize contingency planning), Andrew Grove (plan the way a fire department plans — shape an energetic team capable of responding to the unanticipated), and Ben Horowitz (devote all your time to what you might do, not what you could have done).
points: Great leaders plan to plan again — they treat planning as a living discipline rather than a one-time event, because markets shift, assumptions falter, and disruption can upend a playbook overnight.
Preparation matters but is not enough; institutionalization (consistent routines and dependable processes) is what makes planning durable across the inevitable upheaval.
Pursuing the perfect plan is a trap; focus instead on what's possible with current information and on a flexible framework that enables rapid reassessment and adjustment.

Andrew Grove's fire-department analogy: a fire department can't anticipate where the next fire will be, so it shapes an energetic, efficient team capable of responding to the unanticipated; that is the right model for planning.

Strategic planning is not about predicting and controlling financial outcomes (Rumelt's critique of how most companies actually do it); it's about shaping the organization's response capacity for what hasn't happened yet.
quotes: Great leaders understand that effective planning is essential to move from vision to execution. It's what turns aspiration into action and aligns teams around shared priorities.

Because even the best plans don't survive untouched. Markets shift. Assumptions falter. Global, technological, or competitive disruptions can upend a playbook overnight. That's why the most effective leaders treat planning as a living discipline, not an event.

Rather than pursuing the myth of the perfect plan, focus on what's possible with the current information available. And then develop a flexible framework that enables rapid reassessment and adjustment.

Think of planning as an ongoing conversation, not a one-time declaration of intent. Successful leadership isn't just about making plans; it's about creating a planning culture that embraces structure and flexibility.

The essential problem for most businesses is that their so-called strategic-planning exercises do not produce strategies. Rather, they are actually attempting to predict and control financial outcomes. (Richard Rumelt)

We must recognize that no amount of formal planning can anticipate changes such as globalization and the information revolution. You need to plan the way a fire department plans. It cannot anticipate where the next fire will be, so it has to shape an energetic and efficient team that is capable of responding to the unanticipated as well as to any ordinary event. (Andrew Grove)
Spend zero time on what you could have done, and devote all of your time on what you might do. (Ben Horowitz)” Archived from The Business Leader Daily Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
